title: Patterns & systematic listing
examples: How do I find the next number in this pattern?
Can you show me how to find the number for the tenth figure?
What if the pattern changes halfway through?

explain.say: Look at this pattern of dots on the screen. We need to find the rule.
The first figure has two dots. The second figure has four dots. What is the difference?
It looks like we are adding two dots each time. This is a simple rule we can follow.
If we follow this rule, the third figure should have six dots. We are spotting the pattern.

faq.q: How do I find the number for a very large figure number?
faq.a: If the pattern is consistent, you can use a simple formula to find it. You do not have to draw every single one.
asks: What is the formula for this pattern?
Can I skip ahead in the sequence?

faq.q: What if the pattern changes after a few figures?
faq.a: If the rule changes, you must look closely at the figures before and after the change. Sometimes there is a clue.
asks: Does the rule always stay the same?
How do I know when the pattern breaks?

faq.q: Are there different types of patterns I should know?
faq.a: Patterns can involve adding, subtracting, multiplying, or even alternating between two different rules.
asks: Is this an arithmetic or geometric pattern?
What are the different kinds of rules?

faq.q: Do I need to draw a table for every problem?
faq.a: Making a table helps you organize your thinking and see the numbers clearly. It is a very useful tool.
asks: Should I always use a table?
Is a table necessary for solving this?

faq.q: What if the pattern is based on shapes instead of numbers?
faq.a: You can still use the same thinking. You might count the number of sides or the number of corners instead.
asks: Does this work for shapes too?
How do I count shapes in a pattern?

facts: Patterns are predictable arrangements or sequences.
Finding the rule means figuring out the pattern's pattern.
Tables help organize the given information in a sequence.
The difference between consecutive terms is often the key rule.

quiz.say: Figure 1 has 3 dots. Figure 2 has 5 dots. Figure 3 has 7 dots. Figure 4 should have how many dots?
quiz.why: The pattern is adding two each time, so seven plus two equals nine.

wrong.1: This is tempting because you might be thinking about multiplying by two.
wrong.2: This is a common mistake if you only look at the difference between the first two numbers.
wrong.3: This would mean the pattern is decreasing, which is incorrect here.

quiz.say: A sequence is 2, 5, 8, 11. What is the next number?
quiz.why: The rule is to add three to the previous number to find the next one.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the jump from 11 to 15 is too big for the pattern.
wrong.1: This mistake happens if you only look at the difference between the first two numbers.
wrong.2: This suggests the rule is adding four, which does not fit the start of the sequence.

quiz.say: If Figure 1 has 1 stick and Figure 2 has 3 sticks, what is the total number of sticks in Figure 5?
quiz.why: The pattern adds two sticks each time: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.

wrong.0: This only calculates up to Figure 4, forgetting to find Figure 5.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you kept adding two, but you stopped one step too early.
wrong.3: This mistake might come from adding the first two numbers together incorrectly.
